hints: Focus on what holds a metal together, the attraction between positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
Compare $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Al}^{3+}$ for ion charge and how many outer electrons each atom gives up.
Think how a higher charge and a smaller ion pulled closer to more electrons changes the strength of bonding and melting point.
walkthrough:
**Recall the metallic bond model**

Think of a metal as a lattice of positive ions in a sea of mobile electrons. Melting breaks these strong attractions, so stronger metallic bonding means a higher melting point.

Strength increases with: higher ion charge, more delocalised electrons, smaller ion radius.

**Check statements 1 and 2 from Na to Al**

Sodium forms $\text{Na}^+$, magnesium forms $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, aluminium forms $\text{Al}^{3+}$. So the ion charge increases.

That also means 1, 2 and 3 delocalised electrons per ion respectively, so statement 2 is true.

**Check statement 3 about ion size**

From Na to Al, protons increase from 11 to 13 but electrons are lost to leave the same $2,8$ arrangement. Greater nuclear charge pulls the same shells in more strongly.

So ionic radius decreases: $\text{Na}^+ > \text{Mg}^{2+} > \text{Al}^{3+}$, making statement 3 true.

**Link all three to melting point**

Higher charge, more delocalised electrons and smaller ions all increase charge density and electrostatic attraction between ions and electrons.

Stronger metallic bonding needs more energy to break, so melting point rises from sodium to aluminium. All three statements help explain it.

options.A: Correct. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true and all strengthen metallic bonding. Increasing $\text{Na}^+$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ charge, increasing delocalised electrons, and decreasing radius together explain the rise in melting point.
options.B: Incorrect. This combination includes only 1 and 2. It is tempting to stop there because charge and electron number are the most obvious factors, but it wrongly leaves out the decreasing ionic radius which also strengthens attraction.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination includes only 2 and 3. It misses statement 1, but the increase in ion charge from +1 to +2 to +3 is a key reason the electrostatic attraction to the sea of electrons gets stronger.
options.D: Incorrect. This combination includes only statement 1. Charge alone is not the full story. Students choosing this forget that number of delocalised electrons and ion size also control charge density and bond strength.
